title: Harlem, 1921–1931
subtitle: The Harlem Renaissance from Shuffle Along to the death of A'Lelia Walker — New York, Wilmington and abroad
intro: In May 1921 a Black musical opened on West 63rd Street and ran for more than a year; in June The Crisis printed a short poem about rivers by a nineteen-year-old named Langston Hughes. Over the next ten years Harlem became the place where Black American writers, artists and musicians made a claim on the nation's culture, and where white New York came to watch, buy and judge. This chapter follows that decade from the inside of its rooms: a club dining room on West 12th Street, a Fifth Avenue restaurant, a townhouse salon on 136th Street, a magazine office downtown, a patron's Park Avenue apartment.

Most of the record is letters and dated magazine issues rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. The one true diarist, Alice Dunbar-Nelson, watched from Wilmington, Delaware. Her diary (published in 1984) and her manuscript reading journal log the movement's books, often within days of publication and often on a train, with verdicts of a word or a line. Carl Van Vechten kept daybooks, published in selection in 2003; his entries here rest on his letters and printed introductions. Hughes's own memoir, The Big Sea (1940), is used only where flagged as written later. Because almost all of this material is still in copyright, entries are digests; the few quotations come from magazines printed before 1929.

The hinge of the decade was a set of organised occasions. Charles S. Johnson of Opportunity staged the Civic Club dinner of 21 March 1924 and the awards dinner of 1 May 1925. Alain Locke turned the first into the Survey Graphic Harlem number and The New Negro. The young writers answered with Hughes's manifesto in The Nation and the single fiery issue of Fire!! Patronage ran through all of it: Van Vechten's introductions and contacts, Charlotte Mason's secret stipends and contracts, A'Lelia Walker's open house. The record shows each patron as generous and controlling at once, and the protégés saying so themselves.

The sharpest argument was over what Black art owed its subjects. When Van Vechten published his Harlem novel in August 1926 under a title many readers found wounding, James Weldon Johnson praised it in Opportunity and Hughes defended it. Du Bois called it a caricature and told readers to drop it in the grate. Two years later he said the same of Claude McKay's Home to Harlem, and McKay answered from Barcelona. These are set out as positions held by people who knew and often admired one another. The historic terms appear only in titles and quotations.

The chapter ends with the money gone. The Crash of October 1929 ended much of the white patronage and the downtown visits that had paid for the cabarets and the dinners. Hughes broke with Mason in 1930, his collaboration with Hurston collapsed in Cleveland in February 1931, and A'Lelia Walker died in August. Hughes later chose her funeral as the end of the era, while Dunbar-Nelson's journal for that week lists detective novels.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and need no conversion. Magazine issues (The Crisis, Opportunity, Survey Graphic) are dated by cover month; some appeared days earlier. Where a day is inferred (for example, the Saturday of A'Lelia Walker's funeral) or given differently in different studies (Douglas's December 1925 letter), the entry is marked approximate.

eyes.name: Langston Hughes
eyes.role: Poet, aged 19 when his first major poem appeared in 1921; Columbia student, ship's hand, Paris kitchen worker, Washington busboy, then a Lincoln University student (1926–29)
eyes.side: African American; the younger Harlem writers
eyes.where: Harlem and Columbia (1921–22), at sea and in Paris (1923–24), Washington (1925), Lincoln University, Pennsylvania (1926–29), Westfield and Cleveland (1930–31)
eyes.vantage_label: the poet at the centre of every quarrel
eyes.form: dated letters; published poems and essays; memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: Hughes's letters survive in huge numbers, chiefly in the Langston Hughes Papers at Yale's Beinecke Library; his exchange with Van Vechten (nearly 1,500 letters) was published as Remember Me to Harlem (2001). His account of the decade in The Big Sea (1940) is a memoir written later and is flagged wherever used. Published texts from 1921–28 (The Crisis, The Nation) are dated by issue.
eyes.bio: Hughes arrived in Harlem in September 1921, months after his first great poem appeared in The Crisis, and left and returned several times. He won the Opportunity prize in 1925, published The Weary Blues in 1926, wrote the decade's manifesto in The Nation, accepted and then broke with Charlotte Mason's patronage, and lost his friendship with Hurston over a play. He is the one eye that touches every room in this chapter.

sources.title: Lehigh, African American Poetry: Langston Hughes author page
The Nation: Renaissance Men, by the Letter (Hughes–Van Vechten letters)
The Big Sea, Part III: Black Renaissance (open edition)

eyes.name: Alice Dunbar-Nelson
eyes.role: Poet, journalist and teacher in Wilmington, Delaware, aged 46 in 1921; widow of the poet Paul Laurence Dunbar; columnist and activist
eyes.side: African American; the older generation, at a distance
eyes.where: Wilmington, Delaware, and constantly on trains to Philadelphia, Washington and New York
eyes.vantage_label: a reader of the Renaissance from Wilmington
eyes.authenticity: Her diary survives for 1921 and 1926–31 and was edited by Gloria T. Hull as Give Us Each Day: The Diary of Alice Dunbar-Nelson (Norton, 1984). Separately, her manuscript reading journals, in which she logged each book with date, place and a terse verdict, are transcribed with notes on the University of Delaware's 'Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads' site. Entries here are digests only; neither source is quoted.
eyes.bio: Dunbar-Nelson was a generation older than the Harlem writers and lived a hundred miles away, yet her reading journal tracks the movement book by book, often within days of publication and often on a train. Her one-line verdicts on Van Vechten, McKay, Fisher, Larsen and Hughes form a running review by a sharp, unsentimental reader outside the Harlem salons. Her diary records the money worries and literary disappointments of a working writer.

sources.title: Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (University of Delaware)
Reading journal, 1926
Maryland Humanities: Two Poets and Their Diaries

eyes.name: Carl Van Vechten
eyes.role: White novelist and critic from Iowa, aged 44 in 1924; former music critic; published by Knopf; later a photographer
eyes.side: White American; downtown literary New York
eyes.where: 150 West 55th Street, Manhattan, and Harlem's clubs and parties
eyes.vantage_label: the white patron and novelist in the room
eyes.form: daybooks; dated letters; printed introductions and novel
eyes.authenticity: His daybooks (brief daily notes) were published in selection as The Splendid Drunken Twenties: Selections from the Daybooks, 1922–1930, ed. Bruce Kellner (University of Illinois Press, 2003). His papers are chiefly at Yale's Beinecke Library, with a further collection at the New York Public Library. The entries below rest on his letters, his signed introduction to The Weary Blues and the record of his novel; the daybook pages themselves were not consulted for specific days. His famous portrait photographs date from 1932 onward, after this chapter.
eyes.bio: Van Vechten met Hughes and Cullen on the night Hughes came home in November 1924 and became the Renaissance's most energetic white promoter: he took Hughes's poems to Knopf and wrote the introduction to The Weary Blues. His 1926 Harlem novel, with its deliberately provocative title, split Black opinion. Du Bois condemned it, while James Weldon Johnson and Hughes defended it. Thirteen years earlier he had been in the Paris theatre for The Rite of Spring.

sources.title: University of Illinois Press: The Splendid Drunken Twenties
Lehigh: Van Vechten, Introducing Langston Hughes to the Reader
New York Diaries: Van Vechten

eyes.name: Zora Neale Hurston
eyes.role: Writer and folklorist from Eatonville, Florida; Barnard student from 1925 (BA 1928); anthropological collector under contract to Charlotte Mason from December 1927
eyes.side: African American; the younger Harlem writers
eyes.where: West 139th Street and Barnard (1925–27); the rural South on fieldwork (1927–30)
eyes.vantage_label: prize-winner, editor, then collector in the field
eyes.form: dated letters; published stories and plays
eyes.authenticity: Hurston's letters are collected in Zora Neale Hurston: A Life in Letters, ed. Carla Kaplan (2002); many to Mason, Hughes and Locke survive in their recipients' papers (Howard, Yale). Her autobiography Dust Tracks on a Road (1942) is a memoir written later and is often unreliable on dates; it is not used for dating here.
eyes.bio: Hurston won second prize for fiction at the Opportunity dinner of May 1925 and arrived at its after-party in a way people remembered. Within months she was at Barnard, working for Fannie Hurst, co-editing Fire!!, and then, from December 1927, collecting folklore in the South under a contract that made Mason the owner of what she gathered. Her quarrel with Hughes over Mule Bone in 1931 ended the closest literary friendship of the decade.

sources.title: S&F Online: 'Enter the Negrotarians' (Hurston 1925)
PBS American Masters: Zora Neale Hurston timeline
The Henry Ford: the writing and fallout of Mule Bone

eyes.name: Countee Cullen
eyes.role: Poet, aged 20 in 1924; student at NYU then Harvard (MA 1926); adopted son of the Rev. Frederick A. Cullen of Salem Methodist Episcopal Church; assistant editor and columnist at Opportunity
eyes.side: African American; the younger Harlem writers
eyes.where: Salem M. E. parsonage, Harlem; Paris from summer 1928
eyes.vantage_label: the prize poet who married Du Bois's daughter
eyes.form: dated letters; published poems and columns
eyes.authenticity: Cullen's papers are at the Amistad Research Center (Tulane) and Yale. His Opportunity column 'The Dark Tower' (from late 1926) and his books Color (1925), Copper Sun (1927) and Caroling Dusk (1927) are dated by publication. Details of the 1928 wedding come from the published record of the day.
eyes.bio: Cullen read at the Civic Club dinner in 1924 and was introduced to Van Vechten on the same night as Hughes. He was the movement's most celebrated formal poet and believed a Black poet should not be confined to racial subjects. His 1928 wedding to Yolande Du Bois was Harlem's social event of the decade, and the marriage ended in divorce within two years.

sources.title: Countee Cullen (overview)
Yolande Du Bois (wedding of 9 April 1928)

eyes.name: W. E. B. Du Bois
eyes.role: Editor of The Crisis (NAACP), aged 53 in 1921; historian, sociologist and novelist (Dark Princess, 1928)
eyes.side: African American; NAACP; the older guard
eyes.where: The Crisis office, 69 Fifth Avenue, Manhattan; home in Harlem
eyes.form: signed editorials and reviews in dated monthly issues; dated letters
eyes.authenticity: Du Bois's Crisis pieces are dated by issue and transcribed on the 'Dare You Fight' site; scans of the issues are digitised. His correspondence is in the W. E. B. Du Bois Papers, University of Massachusetts Amherst. Quotations here come only from issues published before 1929.
eyes.bio: Du Bois had published Hughes's first poems and sponsored young writers, but he held that art must also serve truth and justice. In 1926 he ran a symposium on how Black people should be portrayed, gave his 'Criteria of Negro Art' address and condemned Van Vechten's novel; in 1928 he attacked McKay's Home to Harlem in the same issue that praised Larsen's Quicksand. He is the movement's conscience to some and its censor to others; both readings are on the record.

sources.title: The Crisis, Dec 1926, 'Books' (review of Van Vechten's novel)
The Crisis, Oct 1926, 'Criteria of Negro Art'
The Crisis, June 1928, 'Two Novels'

eyes.name: Alain Locke
eyes.role: Professor of philosophy at Howard University, aged 38 in 1924; first African American Rhodes Scholar; editor of the Survey Graphic Harlem number and The New Negro
eyes.where: Howard University, Washington, D.C., with frequent trips to New York and Europe
eyes.vantage_label: the editor who named the movement
eyes.authenticity: The Alain Locke Papers are at the Moorland-Spingarn Research Center, Howard University, and include much of Charlotte Mason's correspondence with him. The Survey Graphic number (March 1925) and The New Negro (December 1925) are dated publications.
eyes.bio: Locke was master of ceremonies at the Civic Club dinner and turned Paul Kellogg's offer into the Survey Graphic Harlem number and then The New Negro, the book that gave the movement its name. He also introduced younger artists, among them Hughes, Hurston and Douglas, to Charlotte Mason, and acted as her go-between. His later critical reviews (including of Fire!!) made him both promoter and judge.

sources.title: Met Museum: Survey Graphic, March 1925 (Locke as editor)
NYPL Digital Collections: Harlem, Mecca of the New Negro

eyes.name: Charles S. Johnson
eyes.role: Sociologist, aged 30 in 1924; director of research for the National Urban League and founding editor of its magazine Opportunity (1923–28); later at Fisk University
eyes.where: Opportunity office, 127 East 23rd Street, Manhattan; Fisk University, Nashville, from 1928
eyes.form: dated letters; magazine issues and anthologies
eyes.authenticity: Johnson's letters to Locke about the Civic Club dinner survive in the Locke Papers (Howard). Opportunity's issues and the prize lists are dated publications. His papers are at Fisk University.
eyes.bio: Johnson saw that literature could win a hearing that sociology could not. He organised the Civic Club dinner of 21 March 1924, ran the Opportunity literary contests, and staged the awards dinner of 1 May 1925 where Hughes, Cullen and Hurston were honoured together. In 1927 he edited the anthology Ebony and Topaz and in 1928 he left New York for Fisk.

sources.title: Charles S. Johnson, 'The Civic Club Dinner, March 21, 1924' (transcription)
CLMP: history of Opportunity

eyes.name: Jessie Redmon Fauset
eyes.role: Literary editor of The Crisis (1919–26), aged 39 in 1921; novelist (There Is Confusion, 1924; Plum Bun, 1929)
eyes.where: The Crisis office, 69 Fifth Avenue, and Harlem
eyes.vantage_label: the literary editor who found the young poets
eyes.form: edited magazine issues; dated letters; novels
eyes.authenticity: Fauset's editorial work is visible in dated Crisis issues; her letters survive chiefly in the Du Bois, Locke and Hughes papers. Her part in discovering Hughes and others is documented in their correspondence and acknowledged in The Big Sea (memoir written later).
eyes.bio: As literary editor of The Crisis, Fauset published Hughes's first poems and encouraged many younger writers. The Civic Club dinner was first planned as a celebration of her first novel, then widened into a showcase for the whole generation. Her novels of middle-class Black life were sometimes overlooked in favour of the cabaret fiction that followed.

sources.title: Civic Club dinner account (Fauset's There Is Confusion)
Dunbar-Nelson's reading journal, 1929 (Plum Bun)

eyes.name: James Weldon Johnson
eyes.role: Executive secretary of the NAACP (1920–30), aged 50 in 1921; poet, novelist, songwriter and former US consul
eyes.where: Harlem (West 135th Street area) and the NAACP office, 69 Fifth Avenue
eyes.vantage_label: the elder statesman who defended the novel
eyes.form: published reviews and books; dated letters; history (written later)
eyes.authenticity: Johnson's papers are in the James Weldon Johnson and Grace Nail Johnson Papers at Yale (Beinecke). His Opportunity review of October 1926 is a dated publication; his account of Harlem in Black Manhattan (1930) is a history written after the events and is flagged where used.
eyes.bio: Johnson bridged the generations: a Broadway songwriter in the 1900s, NAACP leader in the 1920s, and author of God's Trombones (1927) with Aaron Douglas's illustrations. He was Van Vechten's close friend and praised his Harlem novel in Opportunity, the opposite verdict from his NAACP colleague Du Bois. His Black Manhattan (1930) was the first history of the community.

sources.title: Chesnutt to Du Bois, 27 Oct 1926 (mentions Johnson's Opportunity review)
Dunbar-Nelson's reading journal, 1930 (Black Manhattan)

eyes.name: Charlotte Osgood Mason
eyes.role: Wealthy white widow and patron, aged about 73 in 1927; known to her protégés as 'Godmother'
eyes.form: dated letters (largely known through recipients' papers); contract
eyes.authenticity: Mason insisted her patronage stay secret, and her voice survives mainly in letters and memoranda preserved among the papers of Locke (Howard) and Hughes and Hurston. The Hurston contract of December 1927 is known from Hurston scholarship; bell hooks and others have stressed that it made Mason the legal owner of the material Hurston collected. Her total giving to Black artists is estimated at more than $100,000.
eyes.bio: Mason believed Black Americans held a 'primitive' spiritual energy that white civilisation had lost, and she funded artists who she thought could express it. She paid Hughes a monthly allowance from 1927 and financed Hurston's fieldwork, but she wanted control over what they produced. Both relationships ended badly. The record is mostly letters written to or about her, so she is seen largely through those who depended on her.

sources.title: Charlotte Osgood Mason (overview)
Philanthropy Roundtable: Godmother of the Harlem Renaissance

eyes.name: A'Lelia Walker
eyes.role: Heir to and president of the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company (hair-care products), aged 42 in 1927; hostess of the Dark Tower
eyes.side: African American; Harlem business and society
eyes.where: 108–110 West 136th Street, Harlem (the Dark Tower); Villa Lewaro, Irvington
eyes.vantage_label: the hostess whose house was the salon
eyes.form: business letters and invitations; seen chiefly through others
eyes.authenticity: Some of A'Lelia Walker's letters survive in the Madam C. J. Walker papers (Indiana Historical Society), and her great-granddaughter A'Lelia Bundles has published research on her. She kept no known diary; the Dark Tower is described largely through invitations, press reports and guests' later memoirs (Hughes's The Big Sea, 1940). Entries are marked accordingly.
eyes.bio: A'Lelia Walker turned the upper floors of her townhouse into the Dark Tower, named after a Cullen poem. It opened as a private club in October 1927 and closed as a club a year later, though her famous parties went on. Her death in August 1931 was felt by many as the end of an era. Hughes wrote a poem for her funeral and later called her the joy-goddess of Harlem's 1920s.

sources.title: A'Lelia Bundles: A'Lelia Walker's grand Harlem funeral, August 1931
National Trust: How A'Lelia Walker and the Dark Tower shaped the Harlem Renaissance

eyes.name: Claude McKay
eyes.role: Jamaican-born poet and novelist, aged 33 when he left the US in 1922; author of Harlem Shadows (1922), Home to Harlem (1928), Banjo (1929)
eyes.side: Jamaican and African American; expatriate radical
eyes.where: Abroad throughout: Soviet Russia, France (Nice, Marseille, Paris), Spain and Morocco
eyes.vantage_label: abroad, writing Harlem from the Mediterranean
eyes.authenticity: McKay's letters are in the Beinecke (Yale), the Schomburg Center and other collections; a selection was published as Letters in Exile (Yale University Press, 2025), excerpted by The Paris Review. Some letters carry editorial dates in square brackets.
eyes.bio: McKay left the United States in 1922 and spent the whole Renaissance abroad, yet he wrote its first best-selling novel, Home to Harlem. His letters from Nice, Barcelona and Fez comment on Hughes's poems, Van Vechten's introduction, Du Bois's review and the 'Negro intelligentsia', sharply and from far away. He returned to New York only in 1934.

sources.title: The Paris Review: Letters from Claude McKay (2025)

eyes.name: Aaron Douglas
eyes.role: Painter and illustrator from Topeka, Kansas, aged 26 when he came to New York in 1925; pupil of Winold Reiss; illustrator for Opportunity, The Crisis, Fire!!, God's Trombones
eyes.side: African American; the younger Harlem artists
eyes.where: Harlem; Fisk University, Nashville, for the 1930 murals
eyes.vantage_label: the artist who gave the movement its look
eyes.form: dated letters; dated drawings and published illustrations
eyes.authenticity: Douglas's papers are at the Schomburg Center (NYPL) and Fisk University; his letters to Hughes are in the Hughes Papers at Yale. Dates for his illustrations come from the publications that carried them. One letter to Hughes is dated 21 December 1925 in some studies and 25 December in others.
eyes.bio: Douglas came to Harlem in 1925 and, under Winold Reiss's guidance, developed the silhouetted, Africa-inspired style that became the Renaissance's visual signature. He drew for the magazines and for Fire!!, and illustrated James Weldon Johnson's God's Trombones. His letter to Hughes at the end of 1925 states the young artists' aims more directly than anything else in the record.

sources.title: Kirschke, Aaron Douglas and Fire!! (American Studies, KU)
Modernist Magazines: Fire!!

entries.place: Fifth Avenue to Lenox Avenue, Manhattan
entries.headline: Prologue: the 369th marches home up Fifth Avenue
entries.digest: The 369th Infantry, the Black regiment known as the Harlem Hellfighters, paraded from lower Fifth Avenue up into Harlem behind James Reese Europe's band. Johnson later described the march in Black Manhattan as the moment Harlem saw itself honoured by the whole city. The parade is the usual starting point for the decade's new confidence.
entries.source_note: Parade date widely documented; Johnson's account is from Black Manhattan (1930), a history written later and not consulted page by page this session.

entries.headline: Shuffle Along opens on Broadway
entries.digest: Shuffle Along, with music by Noble Sissle and Eubie Blake and a book by Flournoy Miller and Aubrey Lyles, opened at the 63rd Street Music Hall. It ran for 484 performances, to 15 July 1922, and launched Florence Mills and, later, Josephine Baker. Johnson, writing in 1930, counted it among the events that brought white New York uptown.
entries.source_note: NMAAHC, 'Remembering a Milestone in Entertainment History' (opening date, theatre, 484 performances). Johnson's assessment from Black Manhattan (1930), written later.

entries.headline: The Crisis prints 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'
entries.digest: The June Crisis carried a short poem by a nineteen-year-old from Cleveland and Mexico, written on a train crossing the Mississippi. Fauset, as literary editor, had taken it. Its rivers of the Euphrates, Congo, Nile and Mississippi made a single line of descent, and it became Hughes's signature poem.
entries.source_note: The Crisis, June 1921 (Lehigh Hughes author page). Fauset's role from Hughes's correspondence and The Big Sea (memoir written later).

entries.headline: Hughes comes up out of the subway at 135th Street
entries.digest: Hughes arrived to study at Columbia, which his father was paying for, but he wanted Harlem more than the university. In his memoir he wrote that Shuffle Along, then still running, was one of his reasons for coming to New York. He left Columbia after a year.
entries.source_note: Lehigh Hughes author page (fall 1921 Columbia, withdrew June 1922); The Big Sea (1940), memoir written later.

entries.headline: No prize for the Curie sonnet
entries.digest: In late August she had finished a sonnet on Marie Curie for a Philadelphia newspaper's 'favourite woman of the ages' contest, and on 11 September she saw it printed. A week later she learned it had not won. Her diary records the disappointment of a working writer with bills to pay, and she quoted the filmmaker Oscar Micheaux on writing for the public.
entries.source_note: Give Us Each Day (ed. Hull, 1984), entries 27 Aug, 11 Sept and 18 Sept 1921, as described by Maryland Humanities, 'Two Poets and Their Diaries'.

entries.headline: Johnson's dinner for the younger generation
entries.digest: About 110 guests gathered at the Civic Club for an evening Johnson had planned with the Harlem Writers' Guild. It was first intended to celebrate Fauset's novel, but he widened it, as he had argued in a letter to Locke, to present a whole group of new writers to New York's publishers and editors. Before the evening ended, Paul Kellogg of Survey Graphic had offered an entire issue to the new writing.
entries.source_note: Johnson's account and Locke correspondence as transcribed in 'The Civic Club Dinner, March 21, 1924'; National Geographic History (2026).

entries.headline: Locke presides, and is asked to edit an issue
entries.digest: Locke served as master of ceremonies, introducing speakers from Du Bois and James Weldon Johnson to the publisher Horace Liveright and the critic Carl Van Doren. Johnson passed Kellogg's offer of a special Survey Graphic number on to Locke. The dinner turned him from a Washington professor into the movement's chief editor.
entries.source_note: 'The Civic Club Dinner' transcription; Met Museum record for Survey Graphic, March 1925.

entries.headline: A party for There Is Confusion becomes everyone's
entries.digest: Fauset's first novel, There Is Confusion, published by Boni and Liveright, was the occasion of the dinner, and she spoke. But the programme gave most of the evening to others, including Cullen and Gwendolyn Bennett reading poems. Historians have read her later remarks to Locke about the evening as a sign that she felt pushed to the side.
entries.source_note: 'The Civic Club Dinner' transcription; National Geographic History (2026) on Fauset's later letter to Locke. Exact wording of that letter not seen.

entries.headline: Cullen reads to the publishers
entries.digest: Still an NYU undergraduate, Cullen read his poems to a room that included Eugene O'Neill, H. L. Mencken and Zona Gale. Hughes and McKay, the other poets of the moment, were both abroad. Within eighteen months Harper would publish Cullen's first book.
entries.source_note: 'The Civic Club Dinner' transcription (Cullen and Bennett read; Hughes and McKay out of the country).

entries.headline: Walter White introduces two young poets
entries.digest: Van Vechten went uptown to an NAACP benefit dance. Walter White introduced him to Countee Cullen and Langston Hughes, of whom, he later wrote, he had never heard. It was the start of a forty-year friendship with Hughes and of his work as the movement's most visible white promoter.
entries.source_note: Van Vechten, 'Introducing Langston Hughes to the Reader' (introduction to The Weary Blues), via Lehigh anthology; date as given there.

entries.headline: Home from Europe on the day of the dance
entries.digest: Hughes had spent ten months abroad, crewing a freighter to West Africa in 1923 and washing dishes in a Paris nightclub kitchen in 1924. He landed in New York the same day as the NAACP benefit, went uptown, and met Van Vechten. He soon moved to Washington to live with his mother.
entries.source_note: Lehigh anthology (Van Vechten's introduction: arrival and dance the same day); The Nation (ten months abroad).

entries.headline: 'Harlem: Mecca of the New Negro' sells out
entries.digest: The March Survey Graphic appeared with Locke's essays, work by Cullen, Hughes, McKay and others, and Reiss's portraits of Harlem people. It went through two printings and reached some 40,000 readers, more than any previous issue. It was the core of the book Locke would publish in December.
entries.source_note: NYPL Digital Collections, 'Harlem, Mecca of the new Negro' (March 1925); circulation figures from the Civic Club account transcription.

entries.headline: The first Opportunity awards dinner
entries.digest: Johnson presented the prizes of Opportunity's first literary contest at a dinner that brought Black writers together with white judges and publishers. The results set the decade's pecking order: Hughes first for poetry, Cullen second, and Hurston second for fiction with 'Spunk'. The magazine printed the winners over the following months.
entries.source_note: Lehigh anthology, prize-winning poems; S&F Online on Hurston (1 May, second prize for 'Spunk'); National Geographic History (2026).

entries.headline: 'The Weary Blues' takes first prize
entries.digest: Hughes came up from Washington, where he was working menial jobs, and won the poetry prize with 'The Weary Blues', a poem built on the rhythm of a blues player on Lenox Avenue. That spring Van Vechten was already pressing Knopf to publish a collection, and by autumn Hughes had a contract.
entries.source_note: Lehigh Hughes author page (May 1925 prize; Knopf contract in the fall); The Nation on Van Vechten's lunch with Knopf.

entries.headline: Hurston's second prize, and her entrance
entries.digest: Hurston, newly arrived from Howard, took second prize for fiction for 'Spunk', handed to her by the novelist Fannie Hurst, one of the judges. Her arrival at the after-party became a legend among those present. Within months Hurst had hired her as a secretary.
entries.source_note: S&F Online, 'Enter the Negrotarians' (Hurst handed her the award; grand entrance).

entries.headline: Cullen second to Hughes
entries.digest: Cullen took second place for poetry with 'To One Who Said Me Nay'. It was the start of a comparison that followed both poets all their lives: Cullen in strict forms and Hughes in blues measures. That year Cullen also won the Witter Bynner undergraduate prize and published his first book, Color.
entries.source_note: Lehigh anthology prize list; Cullen overview (Witter Bynner first prize 1925; Color, Harper, 1925).

entries.headline: Signing the introduction to The Weary Blues
entries.digest: Van Vechten dated his short introduction to Hughes's first book. It told the story of the meeting in November and of Hughes's wanderings as seaman and kitchen hand, setting the young poet before white readers as a vagabond. McKay and others would find the tone overdone.
entries.source_note: Lehigh anthology: introduction signed New York, 3 August 1925.

entries.headline: Eleven cents and a Barnard bill
entries.digest: In her first term at Barnard, Hurston owed $117 in fees and had eleven cents. She told Annie Nathan Meyer, a Barnard founder, to go ahead and ask Fannie Hurst for help with her tuition. In the first week of November she moved into Hurst's apartment on West 67th Street as her secretary.
entries.source_note: S&F Online, 'Enter the Negrotarians' (17 October go-ahead to Meyer; eleven cents; November move to Hurst's).

entries.headline: The New Negro is published
entries.digest: Locke expanded the Survey Graphic number into an anthology of fiction, poetry, drama, music, art and essays, with decorations and portraits by Winold Reiss and drawings by Aaron Douglas. His title essay argued that a new self-respect was replacing the old image of Black Americans. The book gave the movement its name for a generation.
entries.source_note: Lehigh anthology, 'Front-piece to The New Negro (1925)' (published December 1925; Reiss decorations).

entries.headline: Douglas to Hughes: not white art painted black
entries.digest: Douglas wrote to Hughes that the young artists' task was to create a new art era drawn from the people's own lives, and not to produce white art painted black. He wanted their work to be rooted in the earthy and the everyday. The letter anticipates Hughes's manifesto of the following June.
entries.source_note: Kirschke, American Studies (KU), quoting Douglas to Hughes (Hughes Papers, Yale); the article gives both 21 and 25 December.

entries.headline: The Weary Blues is published
entries.digest: Knopf published Hughes's first collection with Van Vechten's introduction and a cover by Miguel Covarrubias. Vanity Fair had already printed some of the poems. Reviews in the Black press were mixed: some praised the blues poems, others regretted the cabaret subjects.
entries.source_note: Lehigh Hughes author page (January 1926); The Nation (Vanity Fair printed some poems).

entries.headline: McKay thanks Hughes, and grumbles about the introduction
entries.digest: Writing late to thank Hughes for The Weary Blues, McKay praised some poems and named those he disliked. He thought Van Vechten's introduction overdone. He wrote of his money troubles, of reading stories for the film director Rex Ingram, and of his impatience with the Black intelligentsia at home.
entries.source_note: McKay to Hughes, 24 Apr 1926, Letters in Exile (Yale UP, 2025), excerpted in The Paris Review.

entries.headline: 'The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain'
entries.digest: A week after George Schuyler argued in The Nation that there was no distinct Negro art in America, Hughes answered in the same magazine. He wrote that the younger artists meant to express their individual dark-skinned selves without fear or shame. If white or Black readers were displeased, it did not matter. The essay became the generation's manifesto.
entries.source_note: History Matters (GMU): Schuyler, 'The Negro-Art Hokum', The Nation, 16 June 1926, with Hughes's response the following week.

entries.headline: Van Vechten's Harlem novel appears
entries.digest: Knopf published Van Vechten's fifth novel, Nigger Heaven, set among Harlem's professional class and its cabarets. He took the title from the old term for the segregated upper gallery of a theatre or church, and one character applies it to Harlem's place in New York. His own father had warned him against the title, and Johnson and Hughes had urged him to consider others. It sold quickly and went through several printings.
entries.source_note: The Nation (father's warning; Johnson and Hughes suggested alternatives); title meaning from the novel's own usage. Month from Dunbar-Nelson's reading on 9 Sept and the standard bibliographies; day not verified.

entries.headline: Hughes stands by Van Vechten
entries.digest: Hughes defended the novel and its author, then and later. When a copyright claim on song lyrics quoted in the book forced changes, he wrote new verses that replaced them in later printings. In his 1940 memoir he argued that many who condemned the book had not read it. He also argued that it had brought many new readers to Black writers' books.
entries.source_note: Overview of the novel (Hughes's replacement lyrics); The Big Sea (1940), memoir written later. Month of the lyrics not verified.

entries.headline: The Harlem novel, by a white man
entries.digest: Within weeks of publication, Dunbar-Nelson logged Van Vechten's novel. Her one-line note called it the Harlem novel and pointed out, without further comment, that it was written by a white man. The site's editors note that Van Vechten was an acquaintance and admirer of hers.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1926, Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (University of Delaware).

entries.headline: 'Criteria of Negro Art'
entries.digest: The Crisis printed the address Du Bois had given at the NAACP's Chicago conference. He argued that beauty cannot be separated from truth and justice, and that white publishers and audiences decided which Black art was rewarded. His conclusion was that all art is propaganda, and he wanted his to serve the race's fight for recognition.
entries.quote: Thus all Art is propaganda and ever must be
entries.source_note: The Crisis 32 (6), October 1926, pp. 290–97 (Dare You Fight transcription).

entries.headline: Johnson praises the novel in Opportunity
entries.digest: Johnson reviewed his friend's novel favourably in the Urban League's magazine, treating it as a serious novel that showed Harlem's educated and working people as well as its night life. Writers who disliked the book read the review closely. In Cleveland, Charles Chesnutt read it and asked Du Bois what The Crisis would say.
entries.source_note: Chesnutt to Du Bois, 27 Oct 1926 (Chesnutt Archive), confirming Johnson's Opportunity review; summary of its argument from secondary accounts, review not read this session.

entries.headline: Fire!! appears, once
entries.digest: Wallace Thurman's quarterly 'devoted to the younger Negro artists' appeared, priced at a dollar, in about 500 copies, with Douglas's cover designs and drawings. Its board included Hughes, Hurston, Gwendolyn Bennett, Richard Bruce Nugent and John P. Davis. It was meant as a reply to the older generation's respectability. Opportunity welcomed it, The Crisis ignored it, and a Baltimore Afro-American critic singled out Douglas's drawings for scorn.
entries.source_note: Modernist Magazines Project, Fire!!; Lehigh anthology transcription of the issue.

entries.headline: 'Sweat' and Color Struck in Fire!!
entries.digest: Hurston contributed her story 'Sweat', about a washerwoman and her violent husband in a Florida town, and her play Color Struck. She wrote in the rural Black speech she had grown up with, which some older readers disliked. Most unsold copies of the magazine later burned in a basement, and Thurman was left with the debts.
entries.source_note: Lehigh anthology contents; Modernist Magazines Project (fire in the basement).

entries.headline: Du Bois: drop the book in the grate
entries.digest: Du Bois's review called the novel a blow in the face and a caricature built of half-truths. He argued that it presented the cabaret as the whole of Harlem, when most residents were working people who went to church and the movies. He granted that Van Vechten knew Harlem and wrote with skill in places, but he advised readers to drop the book gently in the grate.
entries.quote: an affront to the hospitality of black folk
entries.source_note: The Crisis 33 (2), December 1926, pp. 81–82 (Dare You Fight transcription).

entries.headline: 'Godmother' takes on Hughes
entries.digest: Introduced through Locke, Hughes began receiving support from Mason, a monthly allowance that later sources put at $150. She asked that her name never be used and that he call her Godmother. She wanted him to write out of what she saw as the primitive spirit of his race, and he spent the next years writing his novel Not Without Laughter under her eye.
entries.source_note: Lehigh Hughes author page (1927); Philanthropy Roundtable ($150 a month); Mason overview. Exact month of first meeting not verified.

entries.headline: Fine Clothes to the Jew on a southbound train
entries.digest: Dunbar-Nelson read Hughes's second collection on the train south and recorded no comment. The next day in Roanoke she re-read Du Bois's The Gift of Black Folk. The book's blues poems about porters, prostitutes and workers were attacked in several Black newspapers that winter.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1927, Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (entries 3 and 4 March 1927).

entries.headline: God's Trombones: folk sermons in verse
entries.digest: Dunbar-Nelson logged James Weldon Johnson's seven verse sermons, published by Viking that spring with illustrations by Aaron Douglas. She classed the book as folk sermons in verse. Johnson had turned the cadences of Black preachers into a written poetry without using dialect spelling.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1927, Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (15 May '27).

entries.headline: The Dark Tower opens
entries.digest: A'Lelia Walker opened the Dark Tower as a private membership club in her remodelled townhouse, taking the name from Cullen's poem. The designer Paul Frankl had redecorated the rooms, and his skyscraper bookcase became the club's emblem. Writers, musicians and white downtown guests mixed there.
entries.source_note: National Trust (savingplaces.org), 'How A'Lelia Walker and the Dark Tower shaped the Harlem Renaissance'.

entries.place: New York, then south to Florida and Alabama
entries.headline: The contract with Mason, and the road south
entries.digest: Hurston signed an agreement with Mason that paid her a monthly sum to collect Black folklore, music and religion in the South. Everything she gathered became Mason's property and could be published only with Mason's consent. She drove south in a small car, and over the next two years worked in Florida, Alabama and New Orleans.
entries.source_note: Mason overview citing bell hooks (terms); PBS American Masters (1927 agreement). Day of 8 December from Hurston biographies, not confirmed this session.

entries.headline: A one-word verdict on Home to Harlem
entries.digest: Dunbar-Nelson read McKay's new novel of a Black soldier's return to Harlem's dives within days of publication. Her verdict was a single disgusted word. Later that year she called Rudolph Fisher's The Walls of Jericho the best of the Harlem novels yet.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1928, Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (28 Mar and 14 Jul 1928).

entries.headline: Harlem's wedding of the decade
entries.digest: Cullen married Yolande Du Bois in his father's church. About 1,200 invitations had been sent and some 3,000 people crowded in, with sixteen bridesmaids and Harold Jackman as best man. Two months later Cullen sailed for Paris on a Guggenheim fellowship with his father and Jackman; Yolande followed in August.
entries.source_note: Yolande Du Bois overview (date, place, numbers, Paris).

entries.headline: 'Two Novels': Quicksand praised, Home to Harlem condemned
entries.digest: In one review Du Bois praised Nella Larsen's Quicksand as the best Negro fiction since Chesnutt. He wrote that McKay's Home to Harlem, apart from beautiful passages, catered to a prurient white demand. He said that after its dirtiest parts he felt distinctly like taking a bath.
entries.source_note: The Crisis 35 (6), June 1928, p. 202 (Dare You Fight transcription).

entries.headline: McKay: Du Bois has given me hell
entries.digest: From Barcelona McKay told Hughes he had seen the review, printed in the same Crisis that carried one of his poems. He recalled that the magazine had ignored his earlier work and never returned his other poems. He said he did not mind a fight when he was in the right.
entries.source_note: McKay to Hughes, 13 June 1928, Letters in Exile (Yale UP, 2025), excerpted in The Paris Review.

entries.headline: The Dark Tower closes as a club
entries.digest: A year after opening, the club closed. Walker had begun charging for food and drink, and many of the writers it was meant to welcome could not or would not pay. Her parties continued, but the room was later let out.
entries.source_note: National Trust (savingplaces.org) (closed October 1928).

entries.headline: Plum Bun reaches its readers
entries.digest: Fauset's second novel, about a light-skinned art student who passes for white in New York, was published early in 1929. Dunbar-Nelson logged it simply as a race novel. Two weeks later she read Larsen's Passing on the same theme and grouped it, a little wearily, with the same kind of books.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1929, Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (31 Mar and 14 Apr 1929).

entries.date_display: Tuesday 29 October 1929 (recalled in The Big Sea, 1940)
entries.headline: The Crash, and the end of the vogue
entries.digest: The Wall Street crash ended the money that had paid for downtown visits to Harlem, publishers' advances and private patronage. Writing a decade later, Hughes dated the end of the period when Black people were in vogue to the Depression, which hit Harlem harder than most of the city. Parties grew fewer, and the Dark Tower's rooms had already been let.
entries.source_note: Crash date standard; Hughes's view from The Big Sea (1940), memoir written later; National Trust on fewer parties after 1929.

entries.place: Westfield, New Jersey, and New York
entries.headline: Writing Mule Bone with Hughes
entries.digest: Hurston and Hughes began a folk comedy, Mule Bone, drawn from a tale she had collected, with Louise Thompson, also paid by Mason, typing. By autumn there was a draft, and Hurston went back to fieldwork. In November she sent a version to Van Vechten. Who wrote what became the subject of a quarrel and remains disputed.
entries.source_note: The Henry Ford, 'A Bone to Pick' (spring 1930, Thompson typist, Nov 1930 version to Van Vechten); Westfield location from Hughes scholarship, not confirmed this session.

entries.headline: Not Without Laughter: a mighty good first novel
entries.digest: Dunbar-Nelson read Hughes's first novel, about a Black boy growing up in Kansas, within weeks of publication and praised it warmly. A month later, on a Philadelphia trip, she logged James Weldon Johnson's history Black Manhattan. The novel was the main book Hughes produced under Mason's patronage.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1930, Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (13 Jul and 14 Aug 1930).

entries.date_display: 1930 (break final by the end of the year)
entries.headline: Hughes breaks with Godmother
entries.digest: After three years, Hughes's relationship with Mason ended in a painful scene and an exchange of letters. He felt she wanted to dictate what and how he wrote; she felt he had failed what she believed was his purpose. Hughes later tried to reconcile, without success. The parting was soon followed by his quarrel with Hurston, who remained on Mason's payroll.
entries.source_note: Lehigh Hughes author page (break in 1930); Philanthropy Roundtable (later attempt at reconciliation); Mason overview. Exact date of the final scene not verified.

entries.headline: The Mule Bone quarrel ends a friendship
entries.digest: Recovering from tonsillitis at his mother's home, Hughes learned in January that Cleveland's Gilpin Players had received the script of Mule Bone under Hurston's name alone. A meeting with Hurston in Cleveland on 3 February ended the collaboration and their friendship. Hughes said the play was a joint work; Hurston said it was essentially hers. The play was not staged until 1991.
entries.source_note: The Henry Ford, 'A Bone to Pick with the Writing and Fallout of Mule Bone' (mid-January script; 3 February luncheon; 1991 production).

entries.headline: A'Lelia Walker dies at 46
entries.digest: After a day at the shore celebrating a friend's birthday, A'Lelia Walker died at Long Branch. She was buried at Woodlawn beside her mother. More than 11,000 people filed past her coffin at a Seventh Avenue funeral home the night before the service.
entries.source_note: A'Lelia Bundles, 'A'Lelia Walker's grand Harlem funeral, August 1931'.

entries.headline: A murder mystery the day after
entries.digest: In the days after Walker's death, Dunbar-Nelson's reading journal records detective novels: Agatha Christie's Murder at the Vicarage on 11 August, a mystery about a clergyman's mistress on the 18th, another on the 20th. Nothing in it touches Harlem. By the summer of 1931 her log shows a reader who had turned away from the Harlem novel.
entries.source_note: Reading journal 1931 (continued), Alice Dunbar-Nelson Reads (August 1931 entries).

entries.place: Howell's Funeral Home, Seventh Avenue, Harlem
entries.headline: 'To A'Lelia' is read at the funeral
entries.digest: Hughes wrote a poem for Walker two days after her death, and the critic Edward Perry read it at the invitation-only service. Mary McLeod Bethune gave the eulogy, a quartet sang, and the aviator Hubert Julian dropped flowers from a plane over the grave. In The Big Sea Hughes treated the funeral as the end of the gay times of Harlem's Renaissance.
entries.source_note: A'Lelia Bundles (poem written two days after; read by Perry; Saturday service). Date of 22 August inferred as the Saturday after her death; Hughes's view from The Big Sea (1940), memoir written later.

convergences.label: 21 March 1924: the Civic Club dinner
convergences.note: Johnson organised the evening, Locke presided, Fauset's novel was its pretext, and Cullen read. Du Bois and James Weldon Johnson spoke for the older generation. The organiser saw a launch, while the honoree may have felt sidelined. Hughes and McKay, the absent poets, were in Europe.

convergences.label: 10 November 1924: Hughes lands, and meets Van Vechten
convergences.note: On the day Hughes came home from Europe, Walter White introduced him and Cullen to Van Vechten at an NAACP dance. Van Vechten's printed account and Hughes's later memoir describe the same night from opposite sides of the colour line.

convergences.label: 1 May 1925: the Opportunity awards dinner
convergences.note: One room, three careers. Hughes took first prize over Cullen, and Hurston took second for fiction and made the entrance people remembered. The judges and publishers present turned prizes into contracts within months.

convergences.label: June 1926: manifesto and counter-manifesto
convergences.note: Hughes's Nation essay of 23 June, Douglas's letter of the previous December and Du Bois's Chicago address (printed in October) set out rival programmes. For Hughes and Douglas, art was free self-expression from the people's own life. For Du Bois, all art was propaganda in the service of justice.

convergences.label: August–December 1926: the dispute over Van Vechten's novel
convergences.note: The novel appeared in August, and Dunbar-Nelson logged it on 9 September with a pointed note on the author's race. Johnson praised it in Opportunity in October; Du Bois promised a review on 30 October and condemned it in December. Hughes defended it then and for the rest of his life. The book records these as positions held by people who knew one another well.

convergences.label: November 1926: Fire!!
convergences.note: The younger writers' one-issue magazine, with Douglas's cover and Hurston's 'Sweat', was their answer to respectability. The Crisis ignored it, and most of the unsold copies burned. Du Bois's condemnation of Van Vechten's novel appeared the following month.

convergences.label: April–June 1928: a wedding and a review
convergences.note: Du Bois married his daughter to Cullen in April before thousands. In June the same editor called Home to Harlem nauseating, and McKay wrote from Barcelona to Hughes about the attack. Dunbar-Nelson had already given the novel a one-word verdict in her log in March.

convergences.label: August 1931: A'Lelia Walker's death
convergences.note: Walker died at Long Branch, and Hughes wrote a poem that was read at a funeral thousands tried to attend. Meanwhile Dunbar-Nelson, in Wilmington, was logging murder mysteries. Hughes later made the funeral the symbolic end of the Renaissance; her journal shows how far the Harlem vogue had already faded for one reader.

ties.note: Introduced on 10 November 1924, they exchanged nearly 1,500 letters over forty years; Van Vechten took The Weary Blues to Knopf.
Friends and co-workers on Fire!! and Mule Bone, both funded by Mason; the collaboration and friendship ended in Cleveland on 3 February 1931.
Mason funded Hurston's fieldwork from December 1927 under a contract giving Mason ownership of the material.
Patron and protégé from 1927 to a bitter break in 1930.
Locke was Mason's adviser and introduced Hughes, Hurston and Douglas to her; much of her surviving correspondence is in his papers.
Cullen married Du Bois's daughter Yolande on 9 April 1928; they divorced in 1930.
Du Bois's December 1926 review condemned Van Vechten's Harlem novel; they disagreed publicly over how Black life should be portrayed.
Close friends; Johnson praised the novel in Opportunity in October 1926, taking the opposite position from his NAACP colleague Du Bois.
McKay's letters from Nice (1926) and Barcelona (1928) comment on The Weary Blues, Van Vechten and Du Bois.
Du Bois's June 1928 review condemned Home to Harlem; McKay answered in private letters.
Douglas's letter of December 1925 and their joint work on Fire!! set out the younger artists' aims together.
As literary editor of The Crisis, Fauset published Hughes's first major poem in June 1921.
Johnson organised the Civic Club dinner and handed Kellogg's Survey Graphic offer to Locke.
Hughes attended Walker's parties and wrote 'To A'Lelia' for her funeral in August 1931.

threads_out.note: Van Vechten, who introduced Hughes to Knopf, wrote in Music After the Great War (1915) that he had been in the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées for The Rite of Spring in 1913, with a stranger drumming on his head in time to the music. Twelve years later, in October 1925, the same theatre staged La Revue Nègre with Josephine Baker, who had started out on the road in Shuffle Along's chorus.

The 369th Infantry's victory parade up Fifth Avenue into Harlem on 17 February 1919, behind James Reese Europe's band, is the usual prologue to the Renaissance. Many of the 'New Negro' arguments of the 1920s began with the demand that Black wartime service be repaid with citizenship at home.

Alice Dunbar-Nelson was the widow of Paul Laurence Dunbar, whose father, Joshua Dunbar, had escaped slavery and served in the Union army's 55th Massachusetts Infantry. Du Bois, born in 1868, made Reconstruction the subject of his next great work, Black Reconstruction (1935).
